audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-dominant penultimate, not strict' rests on a one-line pronunciation note in a 1991 SIL language course, quoted correctly (verified verbatim in the now-downloaded Rosetta excerpt, Lesson 1 Pronunciación §1). No better class of source (reference grammar, phonology monograph, instrumental study) exists for this language, but two more authoritative descriptions do exist and were downloaded: Rice 2025 PhD (U Alberta) §2.2.4 'Stress' pp. 73-74 and Nuckolls, Stanley, Nielsen & Hopper 2016 IJAL 82:103-104, 109, 113. Both state penultimate stress as the norm with lexically/morphologically restricted exceptions (3PL -naun final; disyllabic ideophones final; lengthened vowels from elided suffix consonants attract stress; some enclitics such as =mi and topic -ga stress-neutral, yielding antepenultimate; interrogative words antepenultimate per Orr). sources.quote: 'In most Quechuan languages, stress typically falls on the penultimate syllable of polysyllabic words (Adelaar & Muysken 2004: 206). This is largely true of Northern Pastaza Kichwa; however, there are some exceptions.' Exceptions: disyllabic ideophones final; 3PL /-nau̯n/ final; lengthened vowels from suffix-consonant elision attract stress (/wa.ˈsiː/ 'in the house'); 'Otherwise, stress tends to remain on the penultimate syllable, even if heavy syllables are present elsewhere' (ex. 17); enclitics such as =mi do not always shift stress, giving pre-penultimate stress (/ˈnik.pi.mi/); clitic-stres

sources.quote: 'for Quichua verbs, stress is usually placed on the next to last syllable'; verbs shift stress rightward when -chu/-mi are added, whereas 'adverbs (and also adjectives) retain their original penultimate (next to last syllable) stress even after these suffixes are added'; 'stress is a bit irregular for the third person plural forms, shifting to the final syllable ... rather than the penultimate syllable.'

sources.quote: 'In the prosaic lexicon, stress gravitates toward the right edge of a word, with penultimate stress as the most common ... Examples that deviate from this pattern by featuring final stress may be found in verbs inflected for the third-person plural present ending -nawŋ' (103-104); 'Pastaza Quichua words normally receive stress on their penultimate syllables.
